source_text: Consequens erat, ut obseruata dei liberalitate etiam clementiam eius precaremur. quid enim alimenta proderunt, si illi reputamur reuera quasi taurus ad uictimam? sciebat dominus se solum sine delicto esse. docet itaque petamus DI- MITTI NOBIS DEBITA NOSTRA. exomologesis est petitio ueniae, quia qui petit ueniam, delictum confitetur. sic et paenitentia demonstratur acceptabilis deo, quia uult eam quam mortem peccatoris. debitum autem in scripturis delicti figura est, quod perinde iudicio debeatur et ab eo exigatur nec\' euadat iustitiam exactionis, nisi donetur exactio; sicut illi seruo dominus debitum remisit. huc enim spectat exemplum parabolae totius. nam et quod idem seruus a domino liberatus non perinde parcit debitori suo ac propterea delatus penes dominum tortori delegatur ad soluendum nouissimum quadrantem, id est modicum usque delictum, eo competit, quod remittere nos quo- \' que profitemur debitoribus nostris. iam et alibi ex hac specie orationis: remittite, inquit, et remittetur uobis. et cum interrogasset Petrus, si septies remittendum esset fratri, immo, inquit, septuagies septies; ut legem in melius reformaret, quod in Genesi de Cain septies, de Lamech autem septuagies septies ultio reputata est.
thought_title: Forgiveness as confession and the parable of the unforgiving servant
orientation: Tertullian is expounding the fifth petition of the Lord's Prayer, 'Forgive us our debts,' after having treated the petition for daily bread.
pass_a_gloss: It was the next thing, that having observed the generosity of God we should also pray for his mercy. For what will food profit, if we are reckoned to him in truth as a bull for sacrifice? The Lord knew that he alone was without sin. Therefore he teaches that we should ask: FORGIVE US OUR DEBTS. Confession is a petition for pardon, because he who asks for pardon confesses his sin. Thus also repentance is shown to be acceptable to God, because he wants it rather than the death of the sinner. But debt in the Scriptures is a figure of sin, because it is likewise owed to judgment and is exacted from him, nor does it escape the justice of exaction, unless the exaction is forgiven; just as the lord forgave that servant his debt. For to this the example of the whole parable looks. For also the fact that the same servant, freed by his lord, does not likewise spare his own debtor and therefore, denounced before the lord, is handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing, that is, every small sin, fits this, that we also profess to forgive our debtors. Now also elsewhere from this form of prayer: forgive, he says, and it will be forgiven you. And when Peter had asked whether it should be forgiven a brother seven times, no, he says, seventy-seven times; so that he might reform the law for the better, because in Genesis vengeance was reckoned for Cain sevenfold, but for Lamech seventy-sevenfold.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'confession' for exomologesis, understood as confession of sins in the petition for forgiveness.
The glossary requires 'debt' for debitum, understood as sin that requires forgiveness.
Delictum is rendered as 'sin' to keep the moral sense clear, distinct from the financial metaphor of debt.
The Latin phrase literally means 'seventy times seven times,' but the standard English rendering of the Lord's answer is 'seventy-seven times,' matching the Genesis parallel Tertullian draws.
Quadrans is a small Roman coin, rendered 'farthing' as the traditional English equivalent for the smallest coin in the parable.

pass_b_english: It followed that, having observed God's generosity, we should also pray for his mercy. For what good will food do us if we are actually reckoned before him like a bull for sacrifice? The Lord knew that he alone was without sin. So he teaches us to ask: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). Confession is the asking of pardon, because whoever asks for pardon confesses sin. In this way repentance is shown to be acceptable to God, since he desires it rather than the death of a sinner.

In the Scriptures, debt is a figure for sin, because it is likewise owed to judgment and exacted from a person, and it does not escape the justice of exaction unless the exaction is forgiven—just as the master forgave that servant his debt (Matthew 18:27). The whole parable points to this. For the same servant, after being set free by his master, does not likewise spare his own debtor, and for that reason he is denounced before his master and handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing, that is, every sin down to the smallest (Matthew 18:34). This applies to us because we also declare that we forgive our debtors.

And elsewhere, from this same form of prayer, he says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 6:37). And when Peter asked whether he should forgive a brother seven times, he said: “No, seventy-seven times” (Matthew 18:22). He did this to reform the law for the better, since in Genesis vengeance was reckoned sevenfold for Cain, but seventy-sevenfold for Lamech (Genesis 4:24).

problems.quote: handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing—that is, every sin down to the smallest one (Matthew 18:34).
problems.source_quote: delegatur ad soluendum nouissimum quadrantem, id est modicum usque delictum
problems.why: "quadrantem" means a quarter, not a farthing, and the source says "a small sin", not "every sin down to the smallest one".
problems.fix: handed over to the torturer to pay the last quarter, that is, a small sin (Matthew 18:34).

edits.old: handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing—that is, every sin down to the smallest one (Matthew 18:34).
edits.new: handed over to the torturer to pay the last quarter, that is, a small sin (Matthew 18:34).

fixed: Corrected 'farthing' to 'quarter' and 'every sin down to the smallest one' to 'a small sin' to match 'quadrantem' and 'modicum usque delictum'.

problems.why: Source says confession is the asking of pardon, not that the petition is confession.
problems.fix: Confession is the asking of pardon
problems.ruling: Source: "exomologesis est petitio ueniae" = confession is a petition; translation flips to "This petition is a confession".

edits.old: This petition is a confession, because whoever asks for pardon confesses sin.
edits.new: Confession is the asking of pardon, because whoever asks for pardon confesses sin.

fixed: Changed 'This petition is a confession' to 'Confession is the asking of pardon' because the source says 'exomologesis est petitio ueniae' (confession is a petition for pardon), not that the petition is confession.

problems.quote: handed over to the torturer to pay the last quarter, that is, a small sin
problems.why: 'Last quarter' is obscure; 'small sin' as gloss does not clarify.
problems.fix: Render: 'to pay the last penny' (cf. Matt. 5:26) or 'the last farthing'.

edits.old: handed over to the torturer to pay the last quarter, that is, a small sin
edits.new: handed over to the torturer to pay the last farthing, that is, every sin down to the smallest

fixed: The source 'nouissimum quadrantem, id est modicum usque delictum' means 'the last farthing, that is, every sin down to the smallest'. 'Last quarter' is obscure and 'a small sin' misses the sense of 'modicum usque delictum' (every sin down to the smallest). Changed to 'last farthing' and 'every sin down to the smallest'.

last_rejected.quote: does not likewise spare his own debtor
last_rejected.why: perinde here means 'in like manner' or 'correspondingly'—the servant fails to show the same mercy he received, not 'likewise' as mere equivalence.
last_rejected.fix: does not in turn spare his own debtor
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'non perinde parcit debitori suo' means 'does not spare in the same way'; 'does not likewise spare' conveys this adequately.

polish.changed: Clarified the bull-for-sacrifice image by keeping the exact wording but letting the surrounding sentences frame it as a question about the uselessness of food without mercy; broke the long paragraph into three natural turns of thought; made the speaker of the forgiveness sayings unmistakably the Lord; kept every Scripture reference and quotation intact.

notes.quote: we are actually reckoned before him like a bull for sacrifice
notes.why: The image is obscure; reader may not grasp the point.
notes.fix: Clarify: 'like a sacrificial animal awaiting slaughter.'
